I don't know all of this exactly - how it all works - this is general knowledge and not professional legal knowledge - so you should ask an estate Trustee or a lawyer about the exact details.

Technically, the debt is now owed by the estate. All legal property and debts together belong to the estate. The estate is entrusted to a Trustee. The Trustee has the legal responsibility of wrapping up all of the leftover bits of the estate - the will, liquidating assets to pay off debts, payment of back taxes, etc. I think the Trustee also reads the will and sees that the remaining assets are distributed accordingly. Unpaid debtors can sue the estate for settlement of outstanding claims. If the estate cannot cover all of the legitimate claims, the trustee, or a court, must decide the fair distribution of the remaining assets.

As far as debts go in Canada, a debtor can come after anyone for everything except a small amount to live on - that's something like, $5000 or less in the bank, a car to get to work, some furniture and clothes, etc. Basically, it is the same amount of stuff you get to keep if you file for bankruptcy. They can put a lean on major property, such that while they cannot force the sale of it, if it is ever sold then they get paid first. The lean remains as long as the debt remains unpaid. If such a lean is put against the estate, then I imagine it would survive to be passed on to whomsoever should inherit the property.

If there is no actual remaining major property, personal items can be seized by a bailiff to be sold at auction under the direction and supervision of the sheriff. This includes registered used vehicles. Again, the restrictions concerning minimal limits do apply. In this case, personal property of a dead person can be sold at auction - but they will only likely do so if there is value to be found there. All of this activity also costs money - and used household items are basically worthless - collectables, art, etc, might be another matter. How much effort do they want to put into recovering $15K? I suppose that depends on the debtor.

I am fairly sure the Trustee will pay off the debtor, if the Trustee is aware of the debt, before paying out any remaining value towards settlement of the will of the estate. I know the Trustee has to post a public notice in the local paper, and an allotted time period must be observed, and it is within this time period that the debtor must make a claim against the estate if the Trustee is not already informed. Failure to do so within the allotted time cancels the remaining debt, I believe.

In the case of a mortgage, or other outstanding major debt, one should also check the policy for insurance coverage, as many mortgages are insured to automatically pay off in case of death. Home insurance, etc, should also all be checked for death benefits. Even credit card policies, bank account policies, etc. A lot of things financial are covered for the issuer by re-insurance, and that often comes with bonus benefits for things like death, injury, fire, floods, etc. Basically, financial institutions don't take any risks if they can avoid it, and the good deals they offer clients on the front end are often because they are already covered on the back end by their own insurers.

What a debtor cannot do is to pass on the claim for a debt onto the survivors. The debtor can only go after the assets of the estate. The estate is all of the legal property of the deceased.

Pro tip - Canadian bailiffs like to seize property very early in morning:) One way to prevent assets from being seized is if they are not there when the bailiff arrives.
